The world did not end with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a slow, creeping silence. It began in the year 2042, when the global power grid, overwhelmed by the demands of the first wave of artificial superintelligence, began to flicker. Then, it stopped. The satellites fell silent. The internet, that vast nervous system of modern humanity, went dark. And in the aftermath of the "Great Quiet," as historians would later call it, civilization didn’t collapse into chaos; it simply retreated. People moved away from the cities, away from the digital noise, back to the edges of the map.

Among the last remnants of the old world was the lighthouse on Blackrock Point. It was a towering structure of white-painted iron and glass, standing 150 feet above the churning gray waters of the North Atlantic. For decades, it had been automated, its light rotating in a precise, mechanical rhythm, sending out its beacon to ships that no longer needed it. But when the automation failed, the lights went out. And then, the world waited for someone to fix them.

No one came. The coast guard was gone. The maritime authority had dissolved. The ships had stopped coming, mostly. But the sea remained, indifferent and eternal, and the rocks at the base of the lighthouse remained sharp and unforgiving.

Enter Elias Thorne, known to the few scattered communities along the coast simply as Lighthouse Keeper #0.

The wind did not blow at Station Zero; it screamed. It was a low, tectonic moan that vibrated through the iron bones of the tower, a sound that had become so constant to Elias Thorne that he no longer heard it with his ears, but felt it in the marrow of his shinbones.

Elias was the Keeper of Lighthouse #0.

There was no Lighthouse #1, nor #2, nor #3. There was only the Zero. It stood on a jagged, black basalt shelf of rock that jutted out from the mainland like a broken finger pointing at the void. The rest of the coastline was a blur of grey fog and whitecaps, a chaotic ocean that seemed to have no horizon, only an endless churning of slate and storm.

Elias was not a man of the sea. He had been a cartographer once, a man who loved the quiet precision of lines on paper, the certainty of coastlines that did not move. But the world had changed. The "Great Shifting" had erased the maps. The coastlines had liquefied, the land had slipped into the deep, and the only fixed point left in the world was the light of Lighthouse #0. It was the anchor. If the light went out, the ships would not know where the rock was. They would crash. And if the ships crashed, the world would end, for the ships carried the last of the people.

Elias had been at the light for forty years.

He was old now. His hair was a white mane that whipped against his face when he climbed the spiral stairs. His hands were thick, knuckled like driftwood, stained permanently with the black grease of the wick-trimmer
